November 1, 2017 – SOMOS,the Literary Society of Taos, is launching an inaugural literary series titled November Prose Month,with nine evenings of free prose readings by twenty writers. All readings will be held in [SOMOS Salon](http://somostaos.org/capitalcampaign) at 108 Civic Plaza Drive in Taos. Also included in the month-long series are three Saturday workshops focused on the craft of prose writing and performance.
[![Image 1](http://beyondtaos.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2017/11/SOMOS_interior-pano600.jpg)](http://beyondtaos.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2017/11/SOMOS_interior-pano600.jpg)
Jan Smith, SOMOS executive director, explains, “The seed for the prose month concept comes from NaNoWriMo (National Novel Writing Month) which began in 1999. That year, fifteen writers participated. By 2015, participation had soared to over 450,000 writers who signed up to complete 50,000-word prose manuscripts between November 1 and 30.”
The format for November Prose Month follows the organization’s popular April Poetry Month, which gives local and regional poets a platform for reading new and published work to an enthusiastic Taos audience.
Authors will read from prose genres including memoir, creative nonfiction, long and short form novels, flash fiction, mystery/thrillers, and short stories. The schedule of free readings at a glance:

## **Friday, November 3, 7:00pm**
[![Image 2](http://beyondtaos.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2017/11/Iris-Sam.jpg)](http://beyondtaos.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2017/11/Iris-Sam.jpg)
**Sam Richardso**n is a Taos-based artist,storyteller and writer.Before moving to Taos a number of years ago, Sam lived in the Big Bend of Texas where he edited newspapers, was a contributor to state dailies,exhibited in regional art galleries, and operated his own guide service and tour company. His newspaper columns won four Texas press awards.His book about his time in the Big Bend,_Twelve Lessons of the Desert_, has been a consistent seller in Texas markets. His newest books,_Characters Who Never Got Their Own Comic Strip,An Adult Coloring Book_ and _My Little Book of Caricatures, Third Edition_, have been released this year.
**Iris Keltz**’s first book,_Scrapbook of a Taos Hippie: Tribal Tales from the Heart of a Cultural Revolution_(Cinco Puntos Press, 2000) is an award-winning historical memoir documenting the counterculture through vignettes, oral histories, photographs,newspaper articles, and other cultural memorabilia.As a freelance journalist, Keltz’s articles, op-eds, and essays have appeared in print and electronic media, locally, nationally and internationally. She has spoken about the Palestinian-Israeli conflict on radio, in universities, synagogues, churches, high schools, and civic centers, and as part of a national lobby with the Tikkun community in Washington, DC. She is a founding member of Jewish Voice for Peace-Abq and Friends of Sabeel-New Mexico.

![Image 1: Kevin Major - Author, Historian](https://s3.ca-central-1.amazonaws.com/adventurecanada.com-assets2/content/headshots/_100x100_crop_center-center_82_line/kevin-major.jpg)

## Author, Historian
Kevin was conceived a Newfoundlander, but born a Canadian in the year that Newfoundland joined Confederation; he’s been trying to deal with that paradox ever since.
Kevin is an author from Newfoundland. After graduating from Memorial University in 1972, he worked as a teacher before turning to writing full-time in 1989. While he now writes for an adult readership, he is also known as an author of children’s literature, work for which he has been widely awarded and praised. He received the Vicky Metcalf Award for an outstanding body of work in 1992.
Kevin employs a variety of narrative styles and is noted for his use of Newfoundland local colour. In _Hold Fast_(1978, winner of the Governor General’s Award, the Canadian Library Association Award, and adapted for film) and _Far from Shore_ (1980, winner of the Canadian Young Adult Book Award), Kevin traces the destructive changes to traditional outport family life and values brought on by unemployment and modern materialism. _Blood Red Ochre_ (1989) combines the adolescent problem novel, historical fiction, and time-shift fantasy to examine the extinction of Newfoundland's Beothuk people.
Kevin produced a comic fantasy in _Eating Between the Lines_(1991, winner of the Canadian Library Association Book of the Year Award). In it, a teenager literally enters the world of classic books to prevent the dissolution of his parents' marriage and to solve his own romantic problems. The award-winning _The House of Wooden Santas_ (1997) and _Aunt Olga's Christmas Postcards_ (2005) are illustrated children's books for the Christmas season. _Ann and Seamus_ (2003), with artwork by David Blackwood, received eleven award nominations and was made into a folk opera. It is a novel in verse based on the true story of young Ann Harvey, who in 1828 helped to rescue Irish immigrants whose ship was wrecked on the southwest coast of Newfoundland.

## Author, Historian
Kevin's writing for adults ranges across genres. _No Man's Land_ (1995) tells of a bloody WWI battle fought by the Royal Newfoundland Regiment; it has been adapted for the stage and performed frequently. A second wartime novel, _Land Beyond the Sea_ (2019), is set during the sinking of the Cabot Strait ferry S.S. Caribou by a German submarine during WWII. It is the third book in Kevin’s _NewFoundLand_ trilogy of historical novels, the first being _New Under the Sun_ (2011) and the second _Found Far and Wide_ (2016).
Kevin’s history of Newfoundland, _As Near To Heaven By Sea_ (2002), was a Canadian bestseller and was nominated for the Writers’ Trust Non-Fiction Prize. He has recently ventured into crime fiction, with the offbeat private detective and tour guide Sebastian Synard at its centre.
The first book, _One For the Rock_ (2018), is set in St. John’s. It was followed by _Two For the Tablelands_ (2020) and _Three For Trinity_ (2021). Both were nominated for the Howard Engel Award for the best crime novel set in Canada. The fourth in the series _, Four For Fogo Island_, was published in 2022, and the fifth, _Five For Forteau_, in 2023.
Kevin lives and writes in St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador.

## Manushkin, Fran 1942-
**(Frances Manushkin)**
_PERSONAL:_ Surname is pronounced "Ma-_nush_-kin"; born November 2, 1942, in Chicago, IL; daughter of Meyer (a furniture salesman) and Beatrice (Kessler) Manushkin. _Education:_ Attended University of Illinois and Roosevelt University; Chicago Teachers College, North Campus (now Northeastern Illinois University), B.A., 1964. _Religion:_ Jewish. _Hobbies and other interests:_ "Travel, travel, travel! Swimming, bird watching, cat watching, reading, book collecting, snorkeling, theatergoing."
_ADDRESSES: Home and office_—121 E. 88th St., Apt. 4C, [New York](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/new-york), NY 10128. _Agent_—Amy Berkower, Writers House, 21 W. 26th St., [New York](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/new-york), NY 10010. _E-mail_—fran@franmanushkin.com.
_CAREER:_ Writer. Elementary teacher in Chicago, IL, 1964–65; Lincoln Center for Performing Arts, New York, NY, tour guide, 1966; Holt, Rinehart & Winston, Inc., New York, NY, secretary to college psychology editor, 1967–68; Harper & Row Publishers, Inc., New York, NY, secretary, 1968–72, associate editor of Harper Junior Books, 1973–78; Random House Inc., New York, NY, editor of Clubhouse K-2 (student paperback-book club), 1978–80. Mentor to adult writers in [Eastern Europe](https://www.encyclopedia.com/history/historians-and-chronicles/historians-european/eastern-europe) through International Step-by-Step Association.

_SIDELIGHTS:_ Fran Manushkin is the author of numerous books for young readers. Noted for her whimsical imagination and her lovingly drawn characters, Manushkin's works range from such entertaining picture books as _Baby, Moon Dragon_, and _The Tickle Tree_ to novels like _Lulu's Mixed-Up Movie_ and _Val McCall, Ace Reporter?_, both part of her "Angel Corners" series for girls. In addition, she is the author of several books that portray children and their parents celebrating both Jewish and Christian holidays. In a writing career that has spanned over two decades, Manushkin provides young children with a window on a world where even the simplest things are transformed into joyous events.
Born in Chicago, Illinois, in 1942, Manushkin never thought she would grow up to be an author. Instead, upon graduating from high school, she went to college and earned a teaching certificate. After a four-month stint as a substitute teacher, however, Manushkin decided to abandon the idea of a career in teaching. What she really wanted was to live in New York City, and a job at the Illinois pavilion during the 1964 World's Fair got her there. After the fair ended, Manushkin remained in Manhattan and began a new career, this time in publishing. She worked for a series of book publishers, including Holt, Rinehart & Winston, Harper & Row, and Random House, where she met a host of people who inspired her to try her hand at writing books for children.

## WRITIGS:
### NOVELS; "ANGEL CORNERS" SERIES; FOR CHILDREN
Manushkin's first book, _Baby_, was published in 1972; proving perennially popular with readers, it was reissued as _Baby, Come Out!_ in 1984 and has been translated into eight other languages. _Baby_ is the lighthearted story of a not-quite-yet-born baby who decides that Mom's tummy suits her just fine—until Daddy comes home promising kisses that she cannot feel. _Horn Book_ reviewer Sidney D. Long praised Manushkin's first effort as a "special book for mothers-to-be to share with their other children."
"My stories tend to grow from a single image," Manushkin once commented. "_Baby_, for example, blossomed from an image I had in my head of a mother communicating with her newborn baby. That image metamorphosed into a mother communicating with the child she is carrying in her womb. When the child said, 'I don't want to be born,' it just happened. I did not plan it. I didn't have a plot in mind." Before she became a writer herself, Manushkin believed that books "existed in a pure state in author's heads," with their endings perfectly well thought out. "That simply isn't true," she explained. "Books develop according to their own time. You cannot dictate that a book be born; neither can you dictate to a book. Listen," she added, "really listen, and your book will speak."
_Baby_ was the first of many imaginative books that Manushkin has written for children, each one evolving out of an image or idea. In _Swinging and Swinging_ a young girl on a swing soon finds that she has passengers; first a soft, puffy cloud, then the cheery sun, the moon, and a rain of stars join her. As she drifts into a drowsy half-sleep the moon and stars climb back up into the sky and night falls. In _The Tickle Tree_ a young squirrel in the mood for a belly-grabbing tickle gets his friends to stack up and help him reach the top of a feather-leafed palm tree—which causes such a giggle that the animal tower soon topples like a laughing house of cards.

## WRITIGS:
### NOVELS; "ANGEL CORNERS" SERIES; FOR CHILDREN
"Whether you know it or not, every book you write is about yourself," Manushkin explained. "_Hocus and Pocus at the Circus_, for example, is about my sister and myself—but I'm not telling who the nice sister is!" Geared for beginning readers, _Hocus and Pocus at the Circus_ is about two witches—one mean, the other nice—who are busy laying plans for Halloween night. While Hocus plots to cause havoc at a circus, Pocus misspeaks her spells and ends up adding to the circus-goers' fun by turning rubber balls into puppies and herself into a squealing baby pig, and ends the evening by shooting her sister out of a cannon (harmlessly, of course!). A world where magic is possible also figures in _Moon Dragon_, a trickster tale wherein a tiny mouse devises a way to fool a huge, fire-breathing dragon that has eaten everything in sight and now wants the mouse for dessert. Noting that the author's "magic touch invests all her stories," a _Publishers Weekly_ reviewer wrote that _Moon Dragon_ "is one of [Manushkin's] best."

## WRITIGS:
### NOVELS; "ANGEL CORNERS" SERIES; FOR CHILDREN
Manushkin has also written a number of well-received picture books for preschoolers, including _Let's Go Riding in Our Strollers_ and _Peeping and Sleeping_. Featuring a lively, rhyming verse text, _Let's Go Riding in Our Strollers_ presents all of the excitement of the urban outdoors as seen through the eyes of toddlers in strollers on their adventurous trip to the park. _Booklist_ reviewer Ilene Cooper praised Manushkin's "exuberant text" in _Let's Go Riding in Our Strollers_, concluding that the book is "fun to look at and to read." _Peeping and Sleeping_ centers on a peeping noise that is keeping little Barry awake. Barry's father takes the young child out to the pond to investigate, and soon the boy's fears turn to curiosity and wonder at the busy activities of nocturnal creatures. _School Library Journal_ contributor Lisa Wu Stowe praised "Manushkin's wonderfully realistic dialogue and evocative descriptions of a warm spring night's walk" in _Peeping and Sleeping_. A _Publishers Weekly_ reviewer maintained: "Especially well captured is the trembling mixture of fear and giddiness that accompanies children's nighttime excursions." In another favorable estimation, _Booklist_ reviewer Hazel Rochman asserted: "Although rooted in reality, the story with its gentle reversals creates a sense of hidden wonder, of magic and mischief in a hushed nighttime landscape."
Some of Manushkin's books for younger readers are designed as bedtime stories. _The Little Sleepyhead_ features a young troublemaker who, after a day at play, wants to find a soft place to sleep. But grass tickles him, trees are too bumpy, and the bear snores. The child is eventually able to find a bed of feathers, and coaxes a lamb to snuggle with him as he drifts off to sleep. "The last sentence makes it perfect for the last story before bed," noted a critic for _Kirkus Reviews_. A _Publishers Weekly_ contributor noted that Manushkin has created "an appealing toddler-size adventure, casting her spell from the opening words."

Title: Education of a Tour Guide
Chunks: 4,5,6,7,8,9,10
The Library of Congress, I figured, would set the right tone. But I'd forgotten that a century-old fountain, near the entrance to the Jefferson Building, features a nude statue of Neptune and four equally naked male and female companions living it up in what looks like a mythological singles bar.
The kids noticed.
Can you imagine putting a fountain like this in front of a public library anywhere in the United States today? I asked.
Students inspected Neptune and company and shook their heads.
"No way," said one boy.
Why?
Silence.
Are we too uptight? I asked.
More silence.
What a perfect opportunity to discuss political correctness. I wanted the students to have their say. Then again, the statue may have said it all. Judging by the nervous glances I was getting from a couple of the chaperons, maybe it said too much.
So we headed down the street to the Supreme Court.
This is the last stop in the U.S. judicial system, I said from the front steps of the court. About 7,000 cases are appealed here each year, and only 100 or so are actually heard. Some of them can be strange.
Take the case involving a circus performer in Ohio. The man's job was to get shot out of a cannon. When a local television channel showed his entire act during the evening news, he sued the station for violating his intellectual property rights -- and won.
Lesson No. 1 for eighth-graders: Never help yourself to someone else's work.
Another case I thought might interest them had to do with a woman who was kicked out of the University of Missouri's medical school for poor personal hygiene. The Supreme Court sided with the school and upheld the student's dismissal.
Lesson No. 2: Neatness counts.
That one amazed them. This couldn't be the same Supreme Court of the United States that decided all the famous cases they'd heard about in history class.
Could it?
It was easy to see the students were starting to realize something important about Washington, something often overlooked in the presence of so much grandeur: Namely, that no problem, no complaint can ever be too strange or weird not to interest America's top officials and, after due consideration, end up changing the law of the land.
Nobody seemed to care that I hadn't explained the separation
of powers and how a bill becomes law or neglected to mention

the Founding Fathers, who laid the groundwork for the human cannonball's victory in America's highest court.
"Washington is fun!" said Matt Clark, high-fiving me as we walked to the bus.
THE MORE I SAW OF OTHER SCHOOL GROUPS TOURING THE CITY, the more I appreciated the one I was with. I watched rampaging students treat the Franklin D. Roosevelt Memorial like a playground, splashing in the fountains and, at one point, climbing on the statue of FDR sitting in a wheelchair. Park Service employees ignored what was going on, while most teachers didn't appear to care, either.
Tour guides I talked to said crowd control was the hardest part of their job. One explained how she grabbed a student who was goofing off at the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum, and he threatened to sue her.
I was lucky to have good kids, she said.
On our visit to Ford's Theatre, a park ranger spent 20 minutes on stage telling the story of Lincoln's assassination. The account was so vivid he had the students sitting on the edge of their seats, and, when the presentation was over, everyone applauded.
"It's cool to be someplace where history was made," said Nick Hammer, adding that there's not much going on in Sterling.
"Life in Sterling is just blah!" said Jenna Smith. "Nothing ever happens."
That may be one reason, as I would learn later, why a lot of children who grow up there eventually leave. Some, when they get old enough, move away to find work. Others go off to college and never return. Like small towns all over America, Sterling, as Ronald Reagan said of his nearby home town, is a nice place to "go back to," not necessarily stay for your whole life.
"It isn't something you talk about with other kids," said Michael Hermes. "But we think about it."
OVER THE NEXT TWO DAYS WE TOOK A BOAT RIDE ON THE POTOMAC and went to the top of the Washington Monument. At Arlington National Cemetery it surprised me that John F. Kennedy's grave was, for most of the group, just another stop on the tour. The assassinations of the 1960s are ancient history to 13-years-olds.

September 11, 2001, is the key event in their lives, although, being only 8 when 9/11 happened, not many could remember what they were doing at the time. They watched the changing of the guard at the Tomb of the Unknowns and talked about the feelings Arlington evoked. Some said it made them think of the courage of soldiers fighting in Iraq, more than 200 of whom are buried in Arlington.
Back on the bus, teacher Rita Henkel said the class had been through a lot in the years they've been together. The brother of one classmate died, and so did the mother of another. A number of parents lost their jobs when a mill and other businesses closed. Five years ago Sterling's largest factory went bankrupt, putting 1,500 employees out of work. The same problems kids have in other parts of the country -- suicide, drugs, teenage pregnancy -- also happen in Sterling, Henkel said, and when they do, the whole town (pop. 15,451) often feels the effect.
WE PARTED COMPANY AT A METRO STOP, and the St. Mary's bus took off for Illinois. I wondered what the students would remember about Washington. The marble buildings? The Neptune Fountain? Or was it leaving home that mattered most? Would this visit, for many, be the first step in their eventual departure from Sterling?
A week later, I called Henkel to see how the class liked the trip. Everyone was still talking about it, she said. Seeing the nation's capital was something none of them would ever forget.
I should visit Sterling sometime, I said. I'm from Chicago and had never been to that part of the state.
Graduation was in a month, she told me. Could I possibly come then and talk to the students before they received their diplomas?
A graduation speech?
Who hasn't imagined returning to his alma mater and telling a graduating class what life's all about? Of course, I'm no expert, and it wasn't my alma mater, but this might be the closest I'd ever come to an audience of real graduates in caps and gowns.
How could I say no?

MY PLANE LANDED IN CHICAGO JUST BEFORE NOON ON FRIDAY, GRADUATION DAY, and I picked up a rental car. It didn't take long before I was in corn country. Freshly planted fields stretched in all directions. Distant farm buildings could have been islands in a vast agricultural sea. If ethanol ever replaces gasoline as the fuel of choice, this part of the world could become the new Saudi Arabia and Illinois farmers, energy kingpins. Right now, though, their slow-moving tractors were just adding extra time to my drive.
The plan was for me to surprise the students, who would be dressed in their graduation gowns and waiting in a classroom. When I got to the school, Henkel greeted me with a stack of papers. She had asked the class to write their impressions of Washington, and she wanted me to read Danielle Kinser's.
Danielle wrote about our visit to Arlington National Cemetery, which made her think that "any day . . . lives could end in a second." The lesson she took away was to "try new things, take risks. Don't tether yourself to the same routine or people."
She went on: "I once had a dream that I was going to die soon, so I made a video telling people to do everything that I would never get to do (or was too scared or embarrassed to) -- go to the prom, hang out with your parents . . . be yourself, ride an elephant, scuba dive . . . LIVE LIFE!"
I'd made some notes for my speech but now wondered what worthwhile advice I had for a group of graduating eighth-graders? Listen to your parents? Your teachers? Me? When I walked into the room, the students erupted. I felt like the mystery guest on a talk show. I thanked everyone for having me and said I hoped they enjoyed their visit to Washington.
"Like other journeys you'll make in your lives," I told them, "it was a chance to see someplace new, but more than that to see yourselves in a new way. That's why you should never pass up the opportunity to travel, even if it's just around the corner. You never know what you'll see or how it might change your life."
When I finished, the response was subdued. Maybe it was because I wished them good luck in high school, Henkel said. It meant the eighth grade was over, and so was their childhood.

Students left the building in a double line and walked across the street to St. Mary's Catholic Church, where their families were waiting. Awards were given out, teachers thanked, and, after everyone received a diploma, the class invited me to join in photos on the church steps. I got the feeling that years from now people would be asking who the big guy in the back row was. And why were kids slapping him on the back like he had finally graduated?
As girls hugged and boys offered high-fives, I decided to spend the weekend in Sterling. When I lived in Chicago, other parts of Illinois were a mystery. I knew the rest of the state was out there somewhere, but where?
Now I was the tourist.
ON SATURDAY MORNING I DROVE TO THE CORN FARM WHERE AUSTIN RYAN'S FAMILY LIVED. Once out of town the flat land and wide-open spaces made the horizon appear unreachable. The farm had been in the Ryan family for more than 100 years. Austin was looking forward to earning money during the summer detasseling seed corn for local growers. It's hard work in the hot Illinois sun.
"Basically, you pull the tops off the female corn so they can be pollinated by male corn," he explained. Austin liked farming but wasn't sure he wanted to make a career of it.
John Ryan, his father, was hoping he'd change his mind. There are some "hard questions" coming for Austin's generation, he said. And the answers could determine the fate of many rural communities like Sterling.
The economics of farming can be cruel. When Austin's great-grandfather died, relatives who inherited parcels of his land decided to sell their portions. Austin's father, the only one who wanted to farm, had to scrape together enough money to salvage what he could. The hurt feelings that resulted fractured the family.
Austin lost contact with a lot of his relatives when that happened, his father said. "But it certainly simplified our Thanksgivings."
THAT AFTERNOON I WAS INVITED TO MICHAEL HERMES'S HOUSE. On the way I got to see what was happening to Sterling. Stores and businesses were abandoned. One entire shopping center was boarded up, deserted by owners when some of the town's steel mills and factories went bust.

Michael's dad, Jim Hermes, was also a corn farmer. Since his wife's death almost 10 years ago, he's had to raise six children on his own. Michael's older brother, Martin, who's been paralyzed since age 3, when a tree branch fell on him, uses a wheelchair. Another brother is a medical technician in Colorado. One sister has just returned from Africa, where she served in the Peace Corps. The other sister works in Washington.
That's where Michael would like to end up, as a member of Congress.
"If that's what he wants, that's fine," said his father, as he drove us to Reagan's boyhood home in Dixon, 15 minutes from Sterling. The white frame house on a tree-lined street had been totally renovated since the Reagans lived there.
Michael said it's interesting that a president grew up in the area, but, after seeing Washington, Reagan's house wasn't that impressive. Apparently, the Reagans didn't think so, either. They moved three times during the two decades they lived in Dixon.
After going through the house, we went to see Lowell Park, where Reagan had once worked as a lifeguard. The region could use another lifesaver. The local economy was struggling, Jim Hermes said. Wal-Mart just opened a big distribution center, and that's created hundreds of new jobs, but not the kind that will keep his youngest son around when he gets a little older.
"People take what goes on here for granted," the elder Hermes said. "They don't know where their food comes from, and they don't care."
He wasn't blaming Washington, but I assumed he was just being polite.
I CALLED DANIELLE KINSER, who wrote about taking risks and trying new things, to congratulate her for turning in such a good paper.
She told me that visiting Washington was her first trip away from home. Now she couldn't wait to travel to other cities, other countries. But, after she sees the world, Sterling is where she wants to live. She likes the way everyone looks after one another.

Some people think that's the way America used to be, I told her. It still is that way in Sterling, she said. Danielle planned to spend her summer working with Pegasus, a group that helps troubled teenagers and others by teaching them to ride horses. There are a lot of troubled teenagers here, more than you'd think, she added, and the program has only 25 horses.
STERLING'S LEAFY NEIGHBORHOODS and the bandstand in the center of town are what you expect to find in the Midwest. What you don't expect to find is a place fighting for its existence. Before leaving for the airport in Chicago, I met Dan Wahl and his parents for Sunday breakfast. Kids in Sterling have a lot of reality to deal with, I said. The Wahls agreed, putting the economic survival of their families at the top of the list.
The Wahl family has the same concerns, only on a larger scale. Wahl Clipper Corp., which manufactures haircutting products, had its best year ever last year, but to do so it had to globalize. Pressured by big discount stores to lower prices, Greg Wahl, Dan's father and the company's chief executive, cut costs by shifting some production to a new factory in China.
Over pancakes and eggs, he said his biggest challenge was to keep as many jobs as possible in Sterling, where his grandfather began Wahl Clipper in the 1920s. The company employs roughly 650 people locally, but much of the work these days is being done overseas.
None of this appeared to concern Dan, who was eager to show me through the mansion last lived in by his late grandparents. The Spanish-style house on the north side of town looked like a 1940s movie set, and Dan knew where all the secret passages were.
His mother, Beth, said her son was too young to understand the family business. But before long he might have to run it.
Dan said he hasn't really given that much thought.
"I'm still a kid," he said.
Like the rest of his classmates, he'll be starting high school soon, and when you're just getting out of the eighth grade, that's more than enough to think about.
Bill Thomas is the author of Club Fed: Power, Money, Sex and Violence on Capitol Hill and other books.

_SIDELIGHTS:_ Fran Manushkin is the author of numerous books for young readers. Noted for her whimsical imagination and her lovingly drawn characters, Manushkin's works range from such entertaining picture books as _Baby, Moon Dragon_, and _The Tickle Tree_ to novels like _Lulu's Mixed-Up Movie_ and _Val McCall, Ace Reporter?_, both part of her "Angel Corners" series for girls. In addition, she is the author of several books that portray children and their parents celebrating both Jewish and Christian holidays. In a writing career that has spanned over two decades, Manushkin provides young children with a window on a world where even the simplest things are transformed into joyous events.
Born in Chicago, Illinois, in 1942, Manushkin never thought she would grow up to be an author. Instead, upon graduating from high school, she went to college and earned a teaching certificate. After a four-month stint as a substitute teacher, however, Manushkin decided to abandon the idea of a career in teaching. What she really wanted was to live in New York City, and a job at the Illinois pavilion during the 1964 World's Fair got her there. After the fair ended, Manushkin remained in Manhattan and began a new career, this time in publishing. She worked for a series of book publishers, including Holt, Rinehart & Winston, Harper & Row, and Random House, where she met a host of people who inspired her to try her hand at writing books for children.

### NOVELS; "ANGEL CORNERS" SERIES; FOR CHILDREN
Manushkin's first book, _Baby_, was published in 1972; proving perennially popular with readers, it was reissued as _Baby, Come Out!_ in 1984 and has been translated into eight other languages. _Baby_ is the lighthearted story of a not-quite-yet-born baby who decides that Mom's tummy suits her just fine—until Daddy comes home promising kisses that she cannot feel. _Horn Book_ reviewer Sidney D. Long praised Manushkin's first effort as a "special book for mothers-to-be to share with their other children."
"My stories tend to grow from a single image," Manushkin once commented. "_Baby_, for example, blossomed from an image I had in my head of a mother communicating with her newborn baby. That image metamorphosed into a mother communicating with the child she is carrying in her womb. When the child said, 'I don't want to be born,' it just happened. I did not plan it. I didn't have a plot in mind." Before she became a writer herself, Manushkin believed that books "existed in a pure state in author's heads," with their endings perfectly well thought out. "That simply isn't true," she explained. "Books develop according to their own time. You cannot dictate that a book be born; neither can you dictate to a book. Listen," she added, "really listen, and your book will speak."
_Baby_ was the first of many imaginative books that Manushkin has written for children, each one evolving out of an image or idea. In _Swinging and Swinging_ a young girl on a swing soon finds that she has passengers; first a soft, puffy cloud, then the cheery sun, the moon, and a rain of stars join her. As she drifts into a drowsy half-sleep the moon and stars climb back up into the sky and night falls. In _The Tickle Tree_ a young squirrel in the mood for a belly-grabbing tickle gets his friends to stack up and help him reach the top of a feather-leafed palm tree—which causes such a giggle that the animal tower soon topples like a laughing house of cards.

"The last sentence makes it perfect for the last story before bed," noted a critic for _Kirkus Reviews_. A _Publishers Weekly_ contributor noted that Manushkin has created "an appealing toddler-size adventure, casting her spell from the opening words."

Silence.

More silence.

MY PLANE LANDED IN CHICAGO JUST BEFORE NOON ON FRIDAY, GRADUATION DAY, and I picked up a rental car. It didn't take long before I was in corn country. Freshly planted fields stretched in all directions. Distant farm buildings could have been islands in a vast agricultural sea. If ethanol ever replaces gasoline as the fuel of choice, this part of the world could become the new Saudi Arabia and Illinois farmers, energy kingpins. Right now, though, their slow-moving tractors were just adding extra time to my drive.
The plan was for me to surprise the students, who would be dressed in their graduation gowns and waiting in a classroom. When I got to the school, Henkel greeted me with a stack of papers. She had asked the class to write their impressions of Washington, and she wanted me to read Danielle Kinser's.
Danielle wrote about our visit to Arlington National Cemetery, which made her think that "any day . . . lives could end in a second." The lesson she took away was to "try new things, take risks. Don't tether yourself to the same routine or people."
She went on: "I once had a dream that I was going to die soon, so I made a video telling people to do everything that I would never get to do (or was too scared or embarrassed to) -- go to the prom, hang out with your parents . . . be yourself, ride an elephant, scuba dive . . . LIVE LIFE!"
I'd made some notes for my speech but now wondered what worthwhile advice I had for a group of graduating eighth-graders? Listen to your parents? Your teachers? Me? When I walked into the room, the students erupted. I felt like the mystery guest on a talk show. I thanked everyone for having me and said I hoped they enjoyed their visit to Washington.
"Like other journeys you'll make in your lives," I told them, "it was a chance to see someplace new, but more than that to see yourselves in a new way. That's why you should never pass up the opportunity to travel, even if it's just around the corner. You never know what you'll see or how it might change your life."
When I finished, the response was subdued. Maybe it was because I wished them good luck in high school, Henkel said. It meant the eighth grade was over, and so was their childhood.
texts.8:
Students left the building in a double line and walked across the street to St. Mary's Catholic Church, where their families were waiting. Awards were given out, teachers thanked, and, after everyone received a diploma, the class invited me to join in photos on the church steps. I got the feeling that years from now people would be asking who the big guy in the back row was. And why were kids slapping him on the back like he had finally graduated?
As girls hugged and boys offered high-fives, I decided to spend the weekend in Sterling. When I lived in Chicago, other parts of Illinois were a mystery. I knew the rest of the state was out there somewhere, but where?
Now I was the tourist.
ON SATURDAY MORNING I DROVE TO THE CORN FARM WHERE AUSTIN RYAN'S FAMILY LIVED. Once out of town the flat land and wide-open spaces made the horizon appear unreachable. The farm had been in the Ryan family for more than 100 years. Austin was looking forward to earning money during the summer detasseling seed corn for local growers. It's hard work in the hot Illinois sun.
"Basically, you pull the tops off the female corn so they can be pollinated by male corn," he explained. Austin liked farming but wasn't sure he wanted to make a career of it.
John Ryan, his father, was hoping he'd change his mind. There are some "hard questions" coming for Austin's generation, he said. And the answers could determine the fate of many rural communities like Sterling.
The economics of farming can be cruel. When Austin's great-grandfather died, relatives who inherited parcels of his land decided to sell their portions. Austin's father, the only one who wanted to farm, had to scrape together enough money to salvage what he could. The hurt feelings that resulted fractured the family.
Austin lost contact with a lot of his relatives when that happened, his father said. "But it certainly simplified our Thanksgivings."
THAT AFTERNOON I WAS INVITED TO MICHAEL HERMES'S HOUSE. On the way I got to see what was happening to Sterling. Stores and businesses were abandoned. One entire shopping center was boarded up, deserted by owners when some of the town's steel mills and factories went bust.

Michael's dad, Jim Hermes, was also a corn farmer. Since his wife's death almost 10 years ago, he's had to raise six children on his own. Michael's older brother, Martin, who's been paralyzed since age 3, when a tree branch fell on him, uses a wheelchair. Another brother is a medical technician in Colorado. One sister has just returned from Africa, where she served in the Peace Corps. The other sister works in Washington.
That's where Michael would like to end up, as a member of Congress.
"If that's what he wants, that's fine," said his father, as he drove us to Reagan's boyhood home in Dixon, 15 minutes from Sterling. The white frame house on a tree-lined street had been totally renovated since the Reagans lived there.
Michael said it's interesting that a president grew up in the area, but, after seeing Washington, Reagan's house wasn't that impressive. Apparently, the Reagans didn't think so, either. They moved three times during the two decades they lived in Dixon.
After going through the house, we went to see Lowell Park, where Reagan had once worked as a lifeguard. The region could use another lifesaver. The local economy was struggling, Jim Hermes said. Wal-Mart just opened a big distribution center, and that's created hundreds of new jobs, but not the kind that will keep his youngest son around when he gets a little older.
"People take what goes on here for granted," the elder Hermes said. "They don't know where their food comes from, and they don't care."
He wasn't blaming Washington, but I assumed he was just being polite.
I CALLED DANIELLE KINSER, who wrote about taking risks and trying new things, to congratulate her for turning in such a good paper.
She told me that visiting Washington was her first trip away from home. Now she couldn't wait to travel to other cities, other countries. But, after she sees the world, Sterling is where she wants to live. She likes the way everyone looks after one another.
texts.10:
Some people think that's the way America used to be, I told her. It still is that way in Sterling, she said. Danielle planned to spend her summer working with Pegasus, a group that helps troubled teenagers and others by teaching them to ride horses. There are a lot of troubled teenagers here, more than you'd think, she added, and the program has only 25 horses.
STERLING'S LEAFY NEIGHBORHOODS and the bandstand in the center of town are what you expect to find in the Midwest. What you don't expect to find is a place fighting for its existence. Before leaving for the airport in Chicago, I met Dan Wahl and his parents for Sunday breakfast. Kids in Sterling have a lot of reality to deal with, I said. The Wahls agreed, putting the economic survival of their families at the top of the list.
The Wahl family has the same concerns, only on a larger scale. Wahl Clipper Corp., which manufactures haircutting products, had its best year ever last year, but to do so it had to globalize. Pressured by big discount stores to lower prices, Greg Wahl, Dan's father and the company's chief executive, cut costs by shifting some production to a new factory in China.
Over pancakes and eggs, he said his biggest challenge was to keep as many jobs as possible in Sterling, where his grandfather began Wahl Clipper in the 1920s. The company employs roughly 650 people locally, but much of the work these days is being done overseas.
None of this appeared to concern Dan, who was eager to show me through the mansion last lived in by his late grandparents. The Spanish-style house on the north side of town looked like a 1940s movie set, and Dan knew where all the secret passages were.
His mother, Beth, said her son was too young to understand the family business. But before long he might have to run it.
Dan said he hasn't really given that much thought.
"I'm still a kid," he said.
Like the rest of his classmates, he'll be starting high school soon, and when you're just getting out of the eighth grade, that's more than enough to think about.
Bill Thomas is the author of Club Fed: Power, Money, Sex and Violence on Capitol Hill and other books.
